name: The Gilwell Oak

location.address: Gilwell Park, Bury Road, Chingford, London E4 7QW

access: Free day-visitor access, 9am-6pm daily (closed 20 Dec-3 Jan); sign in at the Syd Kesseler Centre reception on arrival, then follow the Heritage Trail to the Training Ground where the oak stands. Owned by The Scout Association but genuinely open to the public, not members-only.
transport: Chingford station (London Overground), then a footpath/pavement to within 50m of the Gilwell Park drive; roughly 20-25 min walk from the station to the tree.
verify_notes: UK Tree of the Year 2017 (26% of public vote), then UK Tree of the Year overall, then 5th at the European Tree of the Year awards. Species and age disagree between sources: the Scout Association's own page says a 2017 arborist survey (done after the award) put it at roughly 350 years, remarkably healthy for its age; the older nomination text (repeated on Wikipedia) says 450-550 years. Used the 350-year survey figure as more derived/credible, flagged the disagreement. No girth recorded anywhere found. Popular myth says Dick Turpin hid in it; the Scout Association's own page debunks this, noting the tree would only have been ~40 years old in Turpin's time (too small to hide in) -- worth using as the surprising-fact lead, it's an official source correcting its own legend. Historical wrinkle for the writer to handle carefully: the Scout Association's own history page states the CURRENT Gilwell Oak is actually the second tree to carry the name; an earlier 'Gilwell Oak' stood in Branchet Field and 1950s maps show the name moved to the current tree at the edge of the Training Ground. So it is not literally the tree Baden-Powell's first 1919 trainees sat under, though it has carried the identity and the ceremonial role since at least the 1950s. Do not bridge-claim continuity the source itself does not assert. Container: joins London (Chingford is inside Greater London / Waltham Forest, Epping Forest); reachable by London Overground, well within day-trip range, not a standalone destination on its own merits beyond the London page.

name: The Craigends Yew

location.address: Near Gryfebank Avenue, Craigends, Houston, Renfrewshire PA6 7NY, beside the River Gryffe

access: Free, public footpath access on former Craigends Estate ground, now beside a housing estate by the River Gryffe; an internal path is cut through the grove itself. No fee, no fixed hours.
transport: No direct train; nearest station is Johnstone, then bus/taxi, or a bus from Glasgow (roughly 45 min) to stops on Barochan Road/Craig Road near Houston. Not within the ~30 minute day-trip boundary of Glasgow (17 miles / ~45-47 min by bus, no direct train), so this does not join the Glasgow page honestly.
verify_notes: This is a single genetic tree (one male yew) that has spread by layering: branches arch down, root where they touch the ground, and send up new stems, so it reads as a grove but is one specimen with an internal path cut through it -- one collectible point, not an avenue or wood. Recorded in the Ancient Tree Inventory (no. 31486) and shortlisted for Scotland's Tree of the Year 2016. Girth 868 cm measured at 30 cm height in 2016 (scotlands-yew-trees.org and Ancient Tree Forum agree on this figure; Wikipedia's infobox gives '27 feet (8.86 m)', which is an internal unit-conversion inconsistency, 27 ft is actually ~8.23 m -- used the 868 cm figure from the specialist yew sources as primary). Canopy/crown circumference about 100 m now, up from 74 m recorded by Robert Hutchison in 1890 (girth then was 640 cm), which is itself useful corroboration of continuous growth and identity. Age: the sound consensus across sources is 500-700 years. One source (scotlands-yew-trees.org) speculates it could be 800-900 years and links it to the Knights Templar via a 12th-century local landowner, based on extrapolating the 1cm/year average girth-growth rule from the 868cm figure; flagging this as speculative rather than using it, since layering yews grow unevenly and the rule is a rough one even for a simple trunk. Health: 2018 conservation work is described as having left the grove in good health despite some historic vandalism/fire damage and a hollowing main trunk, and the tree was producing new leader growth as of the yew-heritage site's account. Container: does NOT join Glasgow, it is 17 miles / ~45-47 minutes away with no direct train, outside the day-trip boundary. Treated as its own place, Houston/Craigends, under the single-tree-destination exception: comparable in scientific/dendrological renown to Fortingall Yew (already published as its own place), an Ancient Tree Inventory entry, a Tree of the Year shortlist entry, and the subject of a dedicated magazine feature (Judy Dowling, Pro Arb) -- a tree specifically worth the trip for yew/ancient-tree enthusiasts, not merely a fine local tree. Flagging this call for the write pass to weigh rather than treating it as settled.

name: The Fuck Tree

location.address: West Heath, Hampstead Heath, London Borough of Camden

access: Free, on Hampstead Heath, a public park managed by the City of London Corporation, open at all times. West Heath is dense woodland; no path or trunk-level detail confirmed beyond the Wikipedia-sourced coordinate.
transport: Within London; nearest tube/rail is Hampstead (Northern line) or Hampstead Heath Overground, then a walk across the Heath (West Heath sits on the far southwest side, roughly 20-25 min walk from either station).
verify_notes: IMPORTANT EDITORIAL FLAG, not a factual gap: this candidate verifies on the narrow factual bar (alive, public, two independent sources) but its whole claim to notability is social/sexual rather than dendrological, and I think this needs an explicit human/Hidde call before it goes anywhere near a city page, which is outside what a verification pass should decide unilaterally. Facts: a sessile oak on West Heath, Hampstead, named by and for its role as a long-standing gay cruising landmark (its low, prostrate trunk is described as facilitating that use, and the bark is 'buffed smooth' from regular contact). Not literally carved with graffiti as far as either source shows; the name describes its use, not a carving. No age, no girth, no dendrological distinction is claimed by any source: it is an ordinary oak notable purely for cultural/subcultural history (a 2024 Armistead Maupin novel, a 2017 art film, a 2023 gallery soap-sculpture piece, a 2025 ACT UP protest against anti-cruising signage nearby). It is real, alive, sourced and genuinely publicly accessible on open parkland, so it does not fail on any of the hard verification criteria (not dead, not private, not withheld, one collectible point). Whether it fits this site's tone, audience and the 'good afternoon outside' framing is a judgement call about content and brand, not about evidence, and I am leaving that call to whoever assembles this rather than making it myself. Coordinate is Wikipedia/Wikidata-sourced (Q134376041) to six decimals but I could not independently confirm it marks the exact trunk in dense woodland rather than the general area, hence approximate rather than confirmed.

name: The Groton Winthrop Mulberry
access: Free, on The Croft, an open common/meadow in the village managed since it was set up as a charity by the Groton Winthrop Mulberry Trust, whose registered charitable purpose is 'to preserve the land known as The Croft as an open space for the enjoyment of the residents of Groton and adjoining parishes, and to maintain and protect the historic Mulberry tree.' No gate, ticket or booking found in any source; the tree stands behind a protective wooden fence but the Croft itself reads as open common land, not a private garden (one specialist mulberry-register page describes it as 'a private garden' but this conflicts with the charity's own stated public-benefit purpose and the older local-history description of the Croft as a village common, so treat the tree itself as fenced-off-from-touching rather than the site being closed to visitors).
transport: No station in Groton; nearest is Sudbury (about 3 miles/5km away, roughly 10 minutes by car, no direct bus route confirmed). Not within a 30-minute public-transport day-trip boundary of any city on our list as far as could be checked in this pass; likely reached by car only.
verify_notes: Believed planted around 1550 by Adam Winthrop (1498-1562), lord of the manor of Groton after Henry VIII granted it to him in 1544 following the dissolution of the monasteries. Adam was the grandfather of John Winthrop, who led the Puritan fleet to Massachusetts Bay in 1630 and became its first governor; the tree is a minor pilgrimage point for American colonial history because of that link, and the Winthrop family reportedly maintains contact with the village. Age is a documented planting-date estimate ('believed'/'thought'), not a measured dendrological figure, so kept broad (roughly 475 years as of 2026, source gives ~1550 planting). No girth or circumference figure found in any source checked (Morus Londinium, the specialist mulberry register, does not give one for this tree, unusual for that source). Current condition: the trunk has collapsed and the tree is now recumbent and layering (a common survival strategy for ancient mulberries, where fallen branches root and put up new growth), protected by a wooden fence; this is a known, stable state rather than a sign of death, and mulberries are notorious for surviving centuries in this collapsed form (compare the Bethnal Green mulberry, verified elsewhere). Access note flagged above: one source (Morus Londinium) calls the site 'a private garden' while the charity's own registered purpose and an older local-history source both describe the Croft as an open common for the village's enjoyment; the two disagree and neither could be independently confirmed with a site visit, so access is stated honestly with the conflict noted rather than picking a side. Container: Groton is a small Suffolk village with no city of its own; nearest town Sudbury is a few miles off with no easy public-transport link found, so this reads as a standalone destination for anyone specifically interested in Winthrop/Massachusetts colonial history rather than a tree that joins a city page. Flagging the own_place call for the write pass to weigh, same as the Craigends Yew precedent.

name: The Holy Thorn, St John's Churchyard
age_estimate: not documented; grafted from a tree planted in the 1930s

location.address: Church of St John the Baptist, High Street, Glastonbury, Somerset BA6 9DP

access: Free, in the churchyard of the Church of St John the Baptist, Glastonbury High Street; churchyards are open public ground.
transport: In central Glastonbury on the High Street; no railway station in Glastonbury itself (nearest is Castle Cary, about 30-40 min by bus/taxi), but the tree is a short walk from any bus stop in the town centre.
verify_notes: This is a specific, currently-living specimen and needs to be distinguished carefully from other 'Glastonbury Thorn' trees that no longer exist, which is the trap in this lead: the legendary original (said to have grown from Joseph of Arimathea's staff on Wearyall Hill) was destroyed in the English Civil War, probably 1647; a 1951 replacement on Wearyall Hill was vandalised in 2010 and 2012 and entirely removed by the landowner in May 2019 (per Wikipedia); a propagated specimen at Glastonbury Abbey died in 1991 and was removed in 1992. The ONLY specimen Wikipedia documents as currently alive is this one, in St John's churchyard, planted in the 1930s by George Chislett (then head gardener of Glastonbury Abbey) and grafted from earlier stock. It is a form of common hawthorn that flowers twice a year, in winter (around Christmas) and again in spring, unlike ordinary hawthorn. A budded winter branch is cut and sent to the reigning monarch every Christmas, a tradition traced back to 1929 (sent to King George V and Queen Mary) and itself echoing an older tradition of sending a branch to Queen Anne (consort of James I) via James Montague, Bishop of Bath and Wells, in the 1600s; the tradition is reportedly still observed today by the Vicar and Mayor of Glastonbury (Great British Life, dated within the last few years, headlined 'The Glastonbury Holy Thorn lives on...'), which is the best alive-now evidence found. No age or girth figure documented for this individual specimen anywhere found; kept to a decade-scale estimate based on its 1930s planting rather than treating it as ancient, since it is a 20th-century graft rather than a veteran tree. Location precision is approximate: coordinate is for the church itself (Grade I listed, on High Street), not a mapped position within the churchyard for the tree specifically. Container: Glastonbury is a well-known small town (Glastonbury Abbey, Glastonbury Tor, Chalice Well) that could plausibly get its own page with several attractions rather than needing the single-famous-tree exception; flagging for the write pass to decide whether this joins a wider Glastonbury page or ships as its own single-tree entry.

name: Wellington's Wellingtonia

location.address: Stratfield Saye House, Stratfield Saye, Hampshire RG7 2BZ

access: Paid entry: grounds/gardens open on limited seasonal dates (recent pattern: a week in early April and most of August), 10am-5pm, gardens-only ticket around £5; the house itself needs a separately booked, timed tour. Privately owned by the Wellington estate (Stratfield Saye House), not open year-round.
transport: No station at Stratfield Saye itself; nearest is Mortimer or Bramley (both a few miles off) or Reading (roughly 8 miles/20-25 min by car), with no direct public transport route confirmed in this pass. Likely a car/taxi day trip from Reading or Basingstoke rather than walkable from a station.
verify_notes: One of 50 'Great British Trees' selected by the Tree Council in 2002 to mark Queen Elizabeth II's Golden Jubilee, celebrating remarkable trees across the UK; this is the national-recognition hook worth leading with. Named for the 1st Duke of Wellington (died 1852), who lived at Stratfield Saye after buying the estate in 1817 following Waterloo; the genus Sequoiadendron was itself commonly called 'Wellingtonia' in Britain in his honour after his death. Sources disagree slightly on the exact planting: one (via Wikipedia's Great British Trees list) says it was planted in 1857 by the 2nd Duchess of Wellington in memory of the Duke and the Battle of Waterloo; another says Wellingtonia was 'first planted at Stratfield Saye by the second Duke in 1854', shortly after the species' 1853 introduction to Britain. Recorded both rather than picking a winner; either way this specimen is among the very first Wellingtonias planted in the country, since the tree was only introduced from California in 1853. Do NOT confuse this single tree with the separate 'Wellingtonia Avenue' near Camberley/Crowthorne, roughly 10 miles away, a c.1.1km avenue of ~113 trees planted 1865 by Frederick Street as a different memorial to the same Duke; that is a distinct site and is blocked in our leads as an avenue, not a single collectible point. No girth or height figure found for this individual tree in this pass; a geograph photo shows multiple trunks/stems visible near the marked tree ('Wellingtonia trunks, Stratfield Saye'), worth checking on a future pass whether this is one specimen with basal regrowth or several trees planted together, since that would change the collectible-point call. Bonus lead for later, not verified here: the same estate's ground also holds 'Copenhagen's Oak Tree and Grave', where Wellington's Waterloo warhorse Copenhagen is buried beneath an oak, per wellington.co.uk's own visiting page -- a second, independently notable tree at the same site worth a future pass. Container: Stratfield Saye is a private estate near Reading/Basingstoke rather than a town; flagging for the write pass whether it joins a Reading page (if published) or ships as its own place given the paid, limited-season access and its Great British Trees status.

name: The Tolpuddle Martyrs Tree
access: Free, open access on Tolpuddle's village green, managed by the National Trust; Ancient Tree Forum's own site page for it states plainly 'open access'.
transport: No station in Tolpuddle; nearest is Dorchester (roughly 7 miles/6-7 min drive, longer by bus), then a short walk from the village bus stop to the green.
verify_notes: In 1834, six Tolpuddle agricultural labourers met beneath this sycamore to discuss low wages and swear a secret oath, an act that led to their conviction and transportation to Australia; they became known as the Tolpuddle Martyrs and are widely credited as founders of the British trade union movement, so the tree is a genuine landmark of labour history, not merely an old tree. Dendrochronology/ring-count assessment in 2005 put the tree at 320 years old then (so already about 150 years old at the time of the 1834 meetings), which gives roughly 340-341 years as of 2026; treating this as a derived estimate from a documented specialist assessment rather than a guess, and keeping the range broad. One of the 50 Great British Trees selected by the Tree Council in 2002, and shortlisted for England's Tree of the Year in 2015, both strong independent notability signals. Girth recorded as 1.3m (Wikipedia, called 'the largest sycamore in Dorset' at that figure) -- flagging this as worth a sanity check by the writer/a future pass, since 1.3m circumference reads small for a documented ~340-year-old sycamore, though the National Trust's active pollarding regime (removing weight from the crown to prolong the tree's life, aiming to add up to two more centuries) could plausibly keep the trunk slimmer than an unpollarded tree of the same age would be. No independent second girth figure could be cross-checked in this pass; monumentaltrees.com's own page for this tree returned a 403 on fetch (two attempts made, noting per fetch discipline rather than retrying further).

name: The Preston Twin

location.address: Preston Park, Preston Road, Brighton BN1 6SD (northern end of the park)

access: Free, in Preston Park, a public park managed by Brighton & Hove City Council, open at all times.
transport: Preston Park railway station is a short walk (roughly 5-10 min) from the northern end of the park where the tree stands; also reachable from Brighton city centre by bus.
verify_notes: Originally a pair, planted around 1613 (almost certainly as part of a hedgerow) and known locally as the Preston Twins; believed among the oldest and largest English elms in the world, escaping the Dutch elm disease that has otherwise wiped out most of Britain's elms since the 1970s thanks to Brighton's aggressive containment programme (beetle traps, pruning infected branches on sight, root-severing trenches between neighbouring trees). The EASTERN twin was shortlisted for UK Tree of the Year 2018, became infected in 2018 and was felled in December 2019; rather than being removed, it was carved into a gilded sculpture that stands reunited beside its surviving twin, unveiled in spring 2023 (Brighton & Hove City Council news). The WESTERN twin is the one still alive and growing; it was also chosen as one of the 70 Ancient Trees for the Queen's Platinum Jubilee ('Jubilee Ancient Trees'), and itself became infected with elm disease in September 2021, treated by girdling (bark removed around the affected limb to halt the disease) with no guarantee of survival at the time; the 2023 council article about the sculpture's unveiling describes the surviving twin as still standing beside it, which is the most recent alive-now evidence found in this pass. Height over 100ft (30m), width/girth given by Wikipedia as 23ft (7.0m), used here as the girth figure (700cm) though it is possible this described canopy spread rather than trunk girth; flag for a future pass to confirm against monumentaltrees.com's dedicated tree-level pages for 'Preston Twins (nr 1)' and '(nr 2)' if that source becomes fetchable (403'd on this pass, two attempts made). A cutting from the felled eastern twin was planted in Amsterdam in 2008 as a preservation/propagation effort, a nice detail for the story. Location precision approximate: coordinate is for the northern end of Preston Park generally, not a mapped trunk position.
